messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 37
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Database Administrator
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 48

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Somatic (Breathlessness): Difficulty breathing or feeling short of breath, Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure, Visual (Needles/Medical): Medical equipment such as needles or drips
  Maladaptive Strategies: Restrict Eating: control eating strictly to feel in control, Avoid Exercise: Exercise, Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

Vignette:
Michael, a 37-year-old North American man who worked as a database administrator, described his life as having divided cleanly into “before” and “after” the illness that nearly killed him. Before that time, he had been recently divorced and living alone, keeping a careful routine that made work and home feel manageable. The illness began abruptly enough that, when he tried to explain it, he still sounded unsettled by how ordinary the day had seemed at first. What had started with breathlessness became a medical emergency, and he remembered the frightening loss of control in stark, physical fragments: struggling to get air, being rushed through examinations, and seeing needles, tubing, and other medical equipment moving in and out of his body while he was too frightened and too weak to do anything but endure it. Those images stayed vivid for him, and even now he could recall the feel of shortness of breath as the moment his mind linked his own body with danger.

In the weeks that followed, Michael found himself responding intensely to anything that resembled that period. He noticed that if he became winded climbing stairs, on a brisk walk, or even after hurrying across the parking lot to the office, he would suddenly feel a wave of alarm. The sensation of not getting enough air was not just uncomfortable to him; it had the quality of a warning that something terrible was about to happen again. He also became uneasy in medical settings and had a strong urge to avoid hospitals, ambulances, and physical examinations whenever possible. Even seeing medical equipment was enough to unsettle him. Needles, IV drips, and the sight of carts or tools in a clinic waiting room could make him tense up before anyone had touched him. He found procedures especially difficult, because they placed him back in the role he had most dreaded during the illness: lying still while others examined him, with no clear sense that he could protect himself.

As the months passed, Michael developed a set of habits meant to help him feel more in control. He began restricting his eating strictly, telling himself that if he could keep his intake tightly regulated, at least one part of his life would feel orderly and contained. He also started avoiding exercise. He had once tried to keep himself healthy through regular physical activity, but now exertion had become linked in his mind with breathlessness, and breathlessness with emergency. Even minor workouts felt risky to him, so he drifted away from them entirely. At work, this showed up in small but important ways: he would choose routes that kept him away from the hospital building near his office, and he became reluctant to schedule routine checkups, even when he knew he probably should. The avoidance was not dramatic, but it slowly narrowed his world and made ordinary errands feel more complicated than they used to be.

What Michael spoke about most readily in the sessions was the way his body stayed on guard. He said he felt constantly tense and ready to react to danger, as if some part of him were still waiting for the illness to return. He would notice his muscles braced before he even understood what had set him off. When something reminded him of the original experience, his body could react strongly and suddenly. A sensation of tightness in his chest, an unexpected shortness of breath, or the sight of medical gear could send him into a state of immediate physical alarm, and he described these moments with frustration because they seemed to happen before he had time to think. Alongside that, he was aware of intense negative feelings that he found difficult to sit with: fear, horror, anger at how vulnerable he had been, and shame that his body had become so unreliable to him. He did not present these feelings as abstract emotions but as a daily burden he carried in silence, especially since his divorce had left him with less immediate support at home.

Recently, Michael sought help after realizing how much energy he was spending organizing his life around the possibility of another medical crisis. He had delayed appointments, avoided exercise, and monitored his body closely, yet still felt he could never fully relax. What finally pushed him to come in was the sense that he was living as though his body were always one step away from failing him again. He said he wanted to understand why a breathless moment or a medical setting could still make him feel so physically overwhelmed, and he was most afraid that he would be caught unprepared if his body signaled danger again. At the same time, he hoped that treatment might help him move through ordinary life without feeling forced to brace himself for another emergency every time he became short of breath or saw the equipment of medicine.
